probes.title: Train with masked L1 loss to match the absolute-error metric
probes.rationale: The fixed independent metric is disk-masked absolute error, but training_loss minimizes masked squared error. Squaring over-weights large residuals and fits the conditional mean, while L1 fits the conditional median, which is the minimizer of absolute error. This is a one-line change: interfaces, model, and config handling (steps/batch_size/seed) are untouched, compute cost is identical, and the training objective now aligns with the evaluation metric.

probes.title: Keep the verified MSE baseline
probes.rationale: The current pipeline is verified: training loss fell steadily from 0.124 to about 0.033 and validation error 0.1221 beats persistence 0.1265 (skill 0.034). With only 40 optimization steps, L1's constant-magnitude gradients can converge more slowly than MSE, whose gradients scale with residual size and quickly shrink small errors, so the loss swap is not risk-free. Retaining the current source preserves the observed positive skill at zero risk while the L1 variant is evaluated separately.

lessons.lesson: When the evaluation metric is fixed and known (here disk-masked absolute error), training the matching loss (L1) is a principled one-line change, and a speculative risk argument (slower L1 convergence at short step budgets) should not override a controlled A/B result: same seed, same steps, same data, only the loss differs, and the aligned objective won on the fixed metric.
lessons.limits: The gain is modest (~1.3% relative error reduction, 0.12212 to 0.12055) from a single seed on one 142-example validation split; final test data and scores are unavailable, so the improvement may not transfer and could partly reflect seed noise. Training-loss values are on different scales between the MSE and L1 runs and cannot be compared directly across runs. L1's constant-magnitude gradients may behave differently at other step counts or learning rates, and the slightly higher runtime (2.33s vs 1.65s) was not investigated. No untested composition (e.g., L1 plus more steps, Huber/smooth-L1, wider model, different seed) is claimed as an improvement.

probes.title: Zero-init the residual output conv so training starts at the persistence baseline
probes.rationale: Diagnosis from evidence: the residual head is randomly initialized, so step-0 predictions equal the x[:,1:2] skip (the persistence field, as implied by the persistence_error comparator) plus a random correction. The logged losses start at 0.268 and need ~15 of the fixed 40 steps just to fall back to persistence-level error (~0.126) before net learning begins; the curve then plateaus at 0.12-0.13. Change: zero-initialize the final conv's weight and bias when architecture=='residual', making the initial prediction exactly the skip path, so all 40 steps learn corrections from the best available starting point instead of first unlearning a random field. Gradients still flow at W=0 because dL/dW_last equals the upstream grad times nonzero input activations; only the trunk's first gradient is delayed one step, negligible at this budget. The 'plain' architecture path is untouched via the guard. Testable prediction: with identical seed/steps/batch_size, the A/B's first training loss should start near ~0.13 instead of ~0.27. Limits: a hypothesis, not an observed gain; single seed, 142-example validation split, final test data unavailable; competes with the sampling candidate since both target wasted budget inside the fixed 40 steps.

probes.title: Seeded epoch-permutation batching for uniform example coverage
probes.rationale: Diagnosis from evidence: fit draws batch indices with torch.randint, i.e., with replacement. Over the fixed budget of 40 steps x batch 8 = 320 draws from 142 examples, coverage is uneven: expected never-sampled examples are about 142*(1-1/142)^320 ~ 15 (~10% of the data), some examples are drawn 5+ times, and ~18% of batches contain an internal duplicate. With the aligned L1 objective every example contributes constant-magnitude gradient, so unseen examples contribute nothing while over-drawn ones dominate the updates. Change: draw batches without replacement from a torch.randperm permutation produced by the same seeded generator, reshuffling whenever fewer than batch_size indices remain. Every batch stays exactly size 8, steps stay 40, the seed is respected, and coverage becomes near-uniform (essentially every example trained 2+ times). Competes with the zero-init candidate: both attack wasted budget within the fixed 40 steps, one via initialization, one via data order. Limits: a hypothesis, not an observed gain; it also changes the RNG consumption pattern, so per-step losses differ from baseline even before any quality effect; single seed, 142-example validation split, final test data unavailable. If both changes independently help, composing them is a separate untested question.

previous.title: Adopt the tested masked L1 training loss aligned with the absolute-error metric
previous.rationale: Select the verified L1 candidate (stage 8211d6079769fab40d06c7459fe5007e) over the MSE baseline. The comparison is controlled: identical config (architecture=residual, width=8, learning_rate=0.001, steps=40, seed=17, batch_size=8), identical data and split; the only diff is training_loss switching .square() to .abs(). On the fixed disk-masked absolute-error metric over the same 142 validation examples (persistence_error identical at 0.126451 in both runs), error improved from 0.122116 to 0.120553 (~1.3% relative) and skill vs persistence rose from 0.0343 to 0.0466; both runs are verified with learner_metric_matches=true. The mechanism also matches the metric: masked L1 is exactly the training objective whose population minimizer (conditional median) target the evaluation measures, whereas masked MSE fits the conditional mean and over-weights large residuals. The KEEP candidate's stated risk — that L1's constant-magnitude gradients converge too slowly within 40 steps — was directly tested and did not materialize: the L1 training loss fell from 0.268 to roughly 0.12 with a clear downward trend, and validation error decreased. Interfaces build_model(input_shape, config), training_loss(prediction, target, mask), and fit(model, x, y, mask, config) are unchanged, config steps/batch_size/seed handling is preserved, the model stays CPU-sized, and runtime rose only modestly (1.65s to 2.33s).

agent.title: Adopt the verified zero-init residual head; reject permutation batching after a null A/B
agent.rationale: Select the verified zero-init candidate (stage 60c7dd8806f46beb34186ca635a69e85) as the new source and reject the permutation-batching candidate (stage 94a92a332f8803e5481b3fd1ea075ffa). The zero-init A/B is controlled: identical config (architecture=residual, width=8, learning_rate=0.001, steps=40, seed=17, batch_size=8), identical data and split (persistence_error identical at 0.12645146598278637 across all three runs, examples=142), and the only source diff is zero-initializing the final conv's weight and bias under the architecture=='residual' guard; the dedicated seeded generator in fit is untouched, so batch indices are identical across runs and the comparison isolates the initialization. On the fixed disk-masked absolute-error metric, error improved from 0.1205529 to 0.1109156 (~8.0% relative) and skill vs persistence rose from 0.0466 to 0.1229 (~2.6x); both runs verified with learner_metric_matches=true. The candidate's pre-registered prediction was confirmed: the first training loss is 0.1254, essentially the persistence level (~0.126), instead of 0.2678 in the baseline, and final training losses sit at ~0.108-0.113 versus ~0.121-0.125 for the baseline. Mechanism: with a randomly initialized head, the residual output starts as the persistence skip plus a random field, so early steps of the fixed 40-step budget are spent unlearning noise; zero-init makes the step-0 prediction exactly the skip path so every step learns a correction. Gradients still flow because dL/dW of the last conv is nonzero at W=0; only the trunk's first gradient is delayed one step, which the A/B shows is negligible here. The permutation candidate's hypothesis (uniform without-replacement coverage helps under L1) was tested and produced error 0.1205572 vs the baseline's 0.1205529 — a +4.2e-6 difference (~0.004%), a tie within noise — so it is not adopted and with-replacement sampling stays. Interfaces build_model(input_shape, config), training_loss(prediction, target, mask), and fit(model, x, y, mask, config) are unchanged, config steps/batch_size/seed handling is preserved, the model remains CPU-sized, and runtime is 1.98s vs 2.05s. The composition of zero-init with permutation batching is untested and is not claimed as an improvement; it is a candidate for a future controlled A/B.

decision.lesson: Zero-initializing a residual head so the network starts exactly at its skip baseline (here the persistence field) turns wasted early steps into productive ones, and the effect was large and predicted in advance: first training loss at the persistence level (~0.126) rather than ~2x higher (0.268), and validation error 0.12055 -> 0.11092 with skill 0.047 -> 0.123 on the fixed metric. The same round's sampling change (without-replacement epoch permutations) tested a plausible coverage argument and produced a null result (0.120557 vs 0.120553), a reminder that mechanistic stories — about initialization and sampling alike — must be confirmed by same-seed controlled A/Bs on the fixed metric, and that a clean null is informative: keep the simpler baseline when the tested alternative shows no gain.
decision.limits: Single seed (17) on one 142-example validation split; final test data and scores are unavailable, so the ~8% gain may not transfer and could partly reflect seed/split noise despite the controlled design. Zero-init applies only when architecture=='residual'; the plain path is untouched. The trunk receives no gradient on the very first step (last-conv weights start at zero); negligible at 40 steps per the A/B but potentially relevant at much shorter budgets. The zero-init + permutation-batching composition is untested and no improvement is claimed for it. The permutation run's per-step losses are not directly comparable to the baseline because its change alters RNG consumption, whereas the adopted zero-init run shares the baseline's batch stream exactly. Runtime differences (~2.0s) were not investigated.
